question: What is lost, and gained, when every phrase ends by almost stopping?
intro: The darkest key of the cycle, five sharps, in bars only one beat long. A tune tied across the barlines floats over a rolling left hand and keeps coming to rest on fermatas.

sections.label: A′ · the opening returns
sections.mNote: first half’s music heard again, about fifty seconds later

sections.label: Close · ritardando to a held chord

cues.title: A tune tied across tiny bars
cues.text: Each bar is 2/8, a single beat, and five sharps give G♯ minor. The right-hand tune is tied across the barlines, so it floats between bars while the left hand rolls semiquaver figures under the pedal. The first phrase ends on a fermata in bar 8.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 14 (IMSLP #03060): key signature of five sharps, 2/8, p, Ped., tied right-hand quavers, left-hand semiquaver figures, ritard. and fermata in the eighth bar. The report’s global key estimate is E♭ minor (r = 0.87), the minor dominant of G♯ minor, a usual confusion in key estimates; its top pitch classes at 0:00 are E♭ A♭ G, which are D♯ G♯ G.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The music nearly stops, again and again
cues.text: The score ends several phrases on fermatas with a ritardando. In the recording the rate of attacks sinks at about 0:10, 0:35, 1:00 and 1:25, roughly every twenty-five seconds. Count the pauses.
cues.evidence: Report: onsets per second fall to 0.8 at 0:10, 1.2 at 0:35, 1.0 at 1:00 and 0.6 at 1:25 against 2–3 elsewhere; levels −21.2, −25.3, −19.7 and −27.8 dB at those windows. Score pp. 14–15: fermata with ritard. at the ends of several phrases.

cues.title: Written while Clara was away
cues.text: Schumann was engaged to Clara Wieck, but her father opposed the marriage. From December 1837 to April 1838 she gave recitals in Vienna, so she was away when he wrote the Kinderszenen in February and March 1838. He told her of the pieces by letter.
cues.evidence: Clara Schumann (Wikipedia, citing Reich): Vienna recitals December 1837 – April 1838; Friedrich Wieck’s opposition to the engagement. Zwickau catalogue, items 1 and 3: diary entries of February 1838 and the letter to Clara of March 1838; Schumann-Portal (Henle review): composed “wahrscheinlich im Februar und März 1838”.

cues.title: The first half comes back
cues.text: Near 0:56 the opening music returns. The form analysis finds stretches of the first fifty seconds again about fifty seconds later, and the novelty peaks at 0:18 and 1:10 sit the same distance into each half.

cues.title: A title borrowed for a childhood
cues.text: In 1995 the novelist Walter Kempowski published memories of his own childhood under the title Weltschmerz. Kinderszenen fast zu ernst, “world-weariness; scenes from childhood, almost too serious”, and printed this piece in notes at the head of the book.
cues.evidence: Zwickau catalogue 175 Jahre Kinderszenen, item 36: Kempowski’s autobiographical childhood memories (Berlin 1995) titled Weltschmerz. Kinderszenen fast zu ernst, with Schumann’s piece printed at the start of the book.

cues.title: A ritardando onto a held chord
cues.text: The last bars slow with ritardando and hairpins and end on a held chord with a fermata. The report shows the relative level falling from −17 dB at 1:45 to −42 dB at 1:55 and the notes thinning to almost none.
cues.evidence: Report: −17.4 dB at 1:45, −30.3 dB at 1:50, −41.9 dB at 1:55; onsets 1.0, 0.2 and 0.0 per second. Score p. 15, last system: ritar-dan-do, hairpins, fermata over the final chord.

transitions.title: A fermata, then the opening again
transitions.how: The phrase before the return closes on a fermata with a ritardando, as several earlier phrases do. What follows is the opening music again, with the same tied tune over the same rolling left hand, and the same five sharps.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.84 at 0:56, dip at 1:00 (1.0 onsets per second, −19.7 dB). Form analysis: 0:03.5–0:18 matches 0:52.5–1:07, so the opening returns near 0:52–0:56 (the estimate is ±4 s). Score pp. 14–15: fermata with ritard. at each phrase end.

transitions.title: The last phrase fades to a held chord
transitions.to: Close · ritardando to a held chord
transitions.how: The final phrase is marked ritardando over its last bars, with long hairpins that thin the sound, and it ends on a held chord with a fermata. The last fermata is the same device that has closed earlier phrases, but nothing follows it, so a pause that had led on now ends the piece.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.46 at 1:42; level −17.4 dB at 1:45, −30.3 dB at 1:50, −41.9 dB at 1:55; onsets fall to 0.0 per second. Score p. 15, last system: ritar-dan-do and a fermata over the final chord.

composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
